blocks.text: Practice long questions for the whole of Chapter 11 (Human Circulatory System), in the shape of a Board long question: each theory question carries 4 marks (describe, explain, compare, label and describe a structure, give examples), as one 4-mark part or in 1+3 / 2+2 sub-parts. Each question has a full model answer.

blocks.prompt: 1 Describe the position of the human heart in the chest. Describe the structure and functions of the pericardium. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Position: the heart is situated in the middle of the chest cavity, between the lungs. Its back surface is near the vertebral column and its front surface is behind the sternum and rib cartilages. Because it lies between the lungs, the left lung is smaller and has a cardiac notch.

Pericardium: the sac enclosing the heart, separating it from surrounding organs. It has two layers:
• Fibrous pericardium (outer): strong connective tissue; protects the heart against external pressure and shocks and prevents excessive dilation of the heart.
• Serous pericardium (inner): a sac of two layers, (a) the outer parietal pericardium beneath the fibrous pericardium and (b) the inner visceral pericardium (epicardium), closely attached to the heart.

Pericardial cavity: the space between the parietal and visceral pericardium; it contains up to 50 mL pericardial fluid, which lubricates the heart and protects it from infections.

book_ref.quote: It is composed of the following two layers;

blocks.prompt: 2 Describe the four chambers of the human heart and the septa that separate them. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Chambers:
• Two upper thin-walled atria (right and left) receive blood from the body and pass it to the ventricles. The right atrium receives deoxygenated blood through the superior and inferior vena cava; the left atrium receives oxygenated blood through the pulmonary veins.
• Two lower thick-walled ventricles distribute blood to the body. The right ventricle pumps blood to the pulmonary trunk; the left ventricle pumps blood to the aorta. The left ventricle wall is about 3 times thicker than the right because it pushes blood all over the body.

Septa:
• Atrioventricular septum: separates the atria from the ventricles; the tricuspid and bicuspid valves lie in it at the entrances of the ventricles.
• Interatrial septum: separates the left and right atria.
• Interventricular septum: separates the left and right ventricles; it is much thicker than the interatrial septum.
Complete separation of deoxygenated (right side) and oxygenated (left side) blood is maintained.

book_ref.quote: There are four chambers of heart

blocks.prompt: 3 What is a cardiac cycle? Describe its phases with their timings and explain how the heart sounds are produced. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Cardiac cycle: the heart works in continuous cycles; its chambers relax and fill passively from large veins, then contract and propel blood. These alternating relaxations and contractions are one cardiac cycle (one heartbeat).

Phases:
1. Diastole (about 0.4 s): atria and ventricles are relaxed and both atria fill with blood.
2. Atrial systole (about 0.1 s): both atria contract and pass blood through the tricuspid and bicuspid valves into the relaxed ventricles.
3. Ventricular systole (about 0.3 s): the filled ventricles contract and pump blood to the pulmonary arteries and aorta; the tricuspid and bicuspid valves close and the pulmonary and aortic valves open.
In a lifetime the heart beats about 2.5 billion times.

Heart sounds (heard with a stethoscope):
• 'Lubb': when both ventricles contract, the tricuspid and bicuspid valves close.
• 'Dubb': when ventricular systole ends and the ventricles relax, the pulmonary and aortic semilunar valves close.
If valves do not close fully or open narrowly, turbulence is heard as a murmur (a hiss).

blocks.prompt: 4 Heart rate changes with the body's needs. (i) Explain how the brain adjusts the heart rate. (ii) Why and how is an artificial pacemaker used? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
(i) Rate of heartbeat: an average adult heart beats about 70 times per minute and pumps the entire blood volume (about 5 litres) every minute. The normal rate is made and maintained by the pacemaker (SA node) and the AV node. The brain also influences it:
• during fever and exercise, the control centre in the brain sends nerve signals to both the pacemaker and AV node, making them increase the heart rate to cope with the situation;
• when we are asleep or at rest, the brain's control centre slows down their activity.

(ii) Artificial pacemaker: if the flow of electrical impulses is blocked, or the impulses from the SA node are weak, the rhythm of the heartbeat may be delayed or it may stop. In such patients with a weak SA node an artificial pacemaker is used. It is a battery-operated device placed in the body by surgery; it emits electrical signals that trigger normal heartbeats.

book_ref.quote: The normal speed of heartbeat is made and maintained by pacemaker and AV node.

blocks.prompt: 5 Describe the waves, segments and intervals of a normal ECG and the abnormalities each may indicate. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
An ECG records the electrical potentials generated by cardiac impulses, using electrodes on the skin on opposite sides of the heart attached to an electrocardiograph. Its parts:

• P wave: beginning of atrial depolarization, initiated by the SA node; causes atrial contraction. Irregular or absent P waves may indicate arrhythmia.
• PR interval and segment: the PR segment shows completion of atrial depolarization. The normal PR interval is 0.12-0.20 s; a prolonged PR interval (more than 0.20 s) is a first-degree heart block.
• QRS complex: beginning of depolarization of the ventricles; atrial repolarization also occurs now. Abnormal QRS may indicate bundle branch block, ventricular tachycardia or other ventricular abnormalities.
• ST segment: completion of ventricular depolarization, about 0.08 s; depressed in ischemia and elevated in myocardial infarction.
• T wave: beginning of repolarization of ventricles; abnormalities may show electrolyte disturbance; a hyper-acute T wave is the earliest finding of acute myocardial infarction.
• QT interval: from the beginning of QRS to the end of the T wave; normally about 0.40 s.

book_ref.quote: ECG shows the following waves of electrical impulses

blocks.prompt: 6 Some newborns are blue babies. (i) What are blue babies and what causes their condition? (ii) Give reason: the left ventricle has the thickest wall and the heart is felt on the left side. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
(i) Blue babies: some abnormal babies have blueness (cyanosis) of the skin. It is due to mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood between the two atria, so mixed blood is supplied to the body. Causes:
• failure of the interatrial foramen to close during development; it is a temporary opening in the embryonic heart between the right and left atria and normally closes;
• failure of the ductus arteriosus to fully constrict; it is a temporary channel between the embryonic pulmonary artery and aorta and normally constricts.

(ii) The left ventricle pumps blood through the aorta to all parts of the body (except lungs), so its wall is about 3 times thicker than that of the right ventricle, which pumps only to the lungs. Because the left side of the heart is stronger and larger, the heart is usually felt on the left side, although it lies in the middle of the chest between the lungs.

book_ref.quote: Some abnormal babies may have blueness (cyanosis) of skin.

blocks.prompt: 7 Explain how capillaries are suited for exchange of materials. How is interstitial fluid formed? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Capillaries as exchange sites:
• They are formed by division of arterioles, join to form venules and penetrate all tissues, reaching the cellular level; no cell is more than 100 micrometres away from a capillary.
• Their walls are a single layer of endothelial cells; internal diameter about 8 micrometres, so RBCs pass in single line.
• Their total length in an adult is over 80,600 km, giving a huge exchange surface.
• Materials are exchanged between blood and tissues by diffusion or active transport; water and diffusible substances pass through the endothelial cells or the intercellular spaces. Some materials are taken up by endocytosis and passed to the other side by exocytosis.

Interstitial fluid: the pressure within capillaries causes continuous leakage of fluid from blood plasma into tissues. This interstitial fluid consists of water with dissolved nutrients, hormones, gases, wastes and small proteins. Large proteins, RBCs and platelets remain in the capillaries, but some WBCs squeeze out through the intercellular spaces.

book_ref.quote: Capillaries are the sites where materials are exchanged between blood and body tissues

blocks.prompt: 8 Explain how arterioles change the blood supply of a tissue according to its metabolic activity. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Structure: the walls of arterioles have more circular muscles than elastic tissue. Their contraction is under the control of the nervous and endocrine systems.
• Vasoconstriction: contraction of the circular muscles narrows the arterioles and reduces blood flow in them.
• Vasodilation: relaxation of these muscles dilates the arterioles and increases blood flow.

Response to metabolic activity:
• When metabolic activity in a tissue rises, oxygen decreases and carbon dioxide increases in its interstitial fluid.
• In response, the circular muscles of the arterioles in that tissue relax (vasodilation).
• Blood flow increases in these arterioles and in the capillaries, supplying more oxygen and removing more carbon dioxide.
• Decreased metabolic activity causes vasoconstriction of the arterioles, reducing the supply.
Within capillary beds, pre-capillary sphincters at the entry of capillary loops also regulate the flow.

book_ref.quote: Vasoconstriction and vasodilation happen in response to changes in metabolic activity of tissues.

blocks.prompt: 9 Blood moves at different speeds in different vessels. (i) Describe the velocity of blood in different vessels and its cause. (ii) How do veins return blood to the heart at low pressure? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
(i) Velocity of blood:
• highest in the aorta, 450-500 mm/sec;
• falls along the arteries and arterioles and is lowest in capillaries, about 1 mm/sec;
• rises again in venules, veins and vena cavae, 250-300 mm/sec.
These changes result from changes in the total cross section of the vessel system.

(ii) Venous return:
• Veins carry blood from body parts towards the heart; their tunica media is relatively thin and slightly muscular because they do not withstand high pressure.
• Semilunar valves in veins prevent the back flow of blood.
• Contraction of surrounding muscles presses the veins and assists the return of blood.
• Smaller veins join to form larger veins and finally the superior and inferior vena cavae, which pour blood into the right atrium; pulmonary veins empty into the left atrium.

book_ref.quote: The velocity of blood flow is different in different vessels.

blocks.prompt: 10 Define a portal system. Describe the hepatic portal system and explain the role of the liver in it. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Portal system: a circulation in which veins end in capillaries.

Hepatic portal system:
• A large hepatic portal vein collects blood from the spleen and alimentary canal and takes it to the liver, where it ends in capillaries.
• Blood from the liver is taken to the heart through the hepatic veins.
• The system extends from the lower portion of the oesophagus to the upper part of the anal canal.
• It is a component of the systemic circulation.

Role of the liver: the blood coming from the alimentary canal contains substances absorbed from the small intestine. These pass through the liver before going to the heart. The liver removes harmful substances from the blood and absorbs nutrients for storage before sending this blood to the heart.

blocks.prompt: 11 Compare pulmonary circulation with systemic circulation. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: In humans (and all mammals and birds) blood circulates in two main pathways. The heart works as a double pump: its right side drives the pulmonary circulation and its left side the systemic circulation. They are compared in the table.

book_ref.quote: blood circulates throughout body in two main pathways

rows: To and from all cells, tissues and organs except the lungs
Begins at the right ventricle: pulmonary trunk divides into right and left pulmonary arteries
Begins at the left ventricle: aorta carries blood to the body
Arteries carry deoxygenated blood; blood is oxygenated in lung capillaries
Arteries carry oxygenated blood; tissues receive oxygen
Pulmonary venules join to form pulmonary veins, which open in the left atrium
Veins join to form the vena cavae, which open in the right atrium
Driven by the right side of the heart
Driven by the left side of the heart; includes coronary, hepatic portal and renal circulations

blocks.prompt: 12 Explain how the hormones ADH and ANH act in opposite ways to keep blood volume and blood pressure normal. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Long-term regulation of blood pressure is done by hormones that change blood volume by affecting reabsorption of water and salt in the kidneys.

ADH (antidiuretic hormone), when volume and pressure fall:
• A decrease in blood volume and pressure is sensed by special receptors in the brain; they create thirst.
• They stimulate the posterior pituitary gland to secrete ADH.
• ADH stimulates the kidneys to retain more water in blood, excreting less in urine, restoring blood volume and pressure.
• ADH also constricts arterioles, which raises arterial blood pressure.

ANH (atrial natriuretic hormone), when volume rises:
• Endocrine cells in the wall of the right atrium secrete ANH when the atrium is stretched by an increased blood volume.
• ANH speeds up the excretion of salts and water through urine, which lowers blood volume and pressure.

Thus ADH raises and ANH lowers blood volume and pressure, keeping them normal.

book_ref.quote: The long-term regulation of blood pressure is done through hormones.

blocks.prompt: 13 What is coronary angiography? Describe how it is performed and how it is linked to treatment. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Diagnostic tests such as ECG and angiography locate the exact problem in cardiovascular patients and measure the severity of disease.

Coronary angiography: an X-ray examination of the blood vessels or chambers of the heart.
• A physician guides a small tube-like device, a catheter, through the large arteries of the body.
• When the tip of the catheter reaches the opening of the coronary arteries, a special fluid (contrast medium or dye) is injected into the catheter.
• The fluid is visible in the X-ray machine, and pictures (angiograms) of the fluid in the coronary artery are obtained.
• If clots are present in the lumen of a coronary artery, the artery appears narrow.

Link to treatment: by changing the diagnostic catheter to a guiding catheter, physicians can pass instruments into the coronary artery through it; the most common are guide wires and balloon dilation catheters, used in angioplasty.

book_ref.quote: Coronary angiography is an X-ray examination of blood vessels or chambers of heart.

blocks.prompt: 14 Define hypertension. Describe its harmful effects on the brain, heart and kidneys. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Hypertension: a chronic (long-lasting) elevation in blood pressure, when it consistently remains above 140/90.

Effects:
• Blood vessels and brain: chronically high pressure increases the chance of rupture of blood vessels. When this occurs in the brain it is a brain haemorrhage, which damages the delicate structure of the brain.
• Heart: hypertension weakens the cardiac muscles. If prolonged, the heart cannot pump effectively and blood flow cannot meet the needs of tissues; blood may be retained in the heart and lungs. This is congestive heart failure.
• Kidneys: hypertension can damage the nephrons. This leads to further retention of salts and water in blood and therefore further hypertension.

book_ref.quote: Whenever blood pressure is chronically elevated

blocks.prompt: 15 What is thrombosis? Describe its causes and its effects on the heart and brain. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Thrombosis: the formation of a thrombus, a solid mass or plug of blood constituents (clot) in a blood vessel, which may block the vessel wholly or partly.

Causes:
1. irritation or infection of the lining of blood vessels;
2. reduced rate of blood flow due to long periods of inactivity;
3. diseases such as pneumonia, tuberculosis and emphysema.
Atherosclerosis also narrows arteries and increases the risk of thrombus formation.

Effects:
• Thrombosis blocks blood flow to organs.
• A thrombus in the coronary arteries causes a heart attack.
• A thrombus in the vessels of the brain causes a stroke.
• A thrombus may be dislodged and carried to other locations; it is then called an embolus. Formation of a thrombus and its carriage elsewhere is thromboembolism.

book_ref.quote: Thrombosis blocks the blood flow to organs.

blocks.prompt: 16 Describe the functions of the lymphatic system, including the roles of lymph nodes, lymphoid masses and spleen. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
The lymphatic system (lymph vessels, lymphoid masses, lymph nodes and lymph) transports materials and returns them from tissues to blood.

1. Return of fluid: it returns excess fluid, dissolved proteins and other substances to blood. In an average person about three litres more fluid leaves blood capillaries daily; it is absorbed by lymph capillaries and returned to the bloodstream before the blood enters the heart.
2. Absorption of fat: lacteals (lymph capillaries in villi) receive chylomicrons formed from absorbed fatty acids and glycerol.
3. Defence: lymph nodes filter lymph; their lymphocytes and macrophages destroy bacteria and viruses present in lymph.
4. Lymphocyte production: lymphoid masses (in the mucosa and submucosa of the alimentary canal; larger ones are spleen, thymus, tonsils and adenoids) produce lymphocytes.
5. Spleen: filters blood through its macrophages and lymphocytes, which destroy foreign particles and aged RBCs; it also stores RBCs.

book_ref.quote: Lymphatic system also helps to defend body against foreign invaders.

blocks.prompt: 17 Lymph capillaries also absorb fat. (i) What are lacteals and how do chylomicrons reach them? (ii) Describe lymph nodes and explain why they swell in diseases such as mumps. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
(i) Lacteals: the branches of lymph capillaries in the villi.
• Fatty acids and glycerol are absorbed into the epithelial cells of the villi, where they form triglycerides.
• The triglycerides are coated with proteins to form chylomicrons, which enter the lacteals.
• Lymph capillaries are more permeable than blood capillaries, so such larger molecules can enter them.

(ii) Lymph nodes: at certain spots the lymph vessels have masses of connective tissue in which lymphocytes are present; these are lymph nodes.
• Several afferent lymph vessels enter a node and the lymph is drained by a single efferent lymph vessel.
• They are present in the neck region, axilla and groin.
• They filter lymph; their lymphocytes and macrophages destroy bacteria and viruses.
• Swelling: the painful swelling of lymph nodes in diseases such as mumps is largely the result of accumulation of dead lymphocytes and macrophages.

book_ref.quote: The branches of lymph capillaries in villi, are called lacteals.
